html:
The Kingdom of Benin was an Edo kingdom in the forest of southern Nigeria, ruled by a king called the Oba from the city of Edo, now Benin City. It has no link to the modern Republic of Benin, which was called Dahomey until 1975.

It grew out of an earlier Edo state, Igodomigodo, around the 1000s and 1100s. Benin tradition links the present royal line to Ife, the Yoruba holy city. In the mid-1400s Oba Ewuare rebuilt the capital and expanded the state, and the 1400s and 1500s were its height. Great earthworks, the walls of Benin, ringed the city and its farmland.

Portuguese ships arrived in the 1480s. Benin sold pepper, ivory, cloth and, for a time, captives, and bought brass, guns and cowries. The brass fed the royal guild of casters who made the Benin Bronzes, plaques and heads that recorded the court and its history.

From the 1700s its reach shrank, though the Oba kept strict control of trade with Europeans. In 1897, after a British party trying to reach the city was attacked and most of its members killed, a British punitive expedition took Benin City, burned much of it, carried off thousands of artworks and exiled Oba Ovonramwen. The kingdom became part of a British protectorate and later of Nigeria, within the British Empire. The monarchy was restored in 1914 and continues today as a traditional office.
sum: The Kingdom of Benin was an Edo kingdom in the forest of southern Nigeria, ruled by a king called the Oba from the city of Edo, now Benin City. It has no link to the modern Republic of Benin, which was called Dahomey until 1975.
